Reviewer #1:

In this manuscript the authors show that the exchange factor for Arf6 (EFa6) functions in depolymerizing microtubules (MTs) in axons to keep MTs bundled in the axon shaft. This is a well-documented and quantified study that adds to our knowledge of this protein in nervous system function. Although the authors show that the full-length protein and the MT-eliminating domain (MTED) serve to depolymerize MTs in the axon and growth cone, they are not able to discern the molecular mechanism by which this protein and domain function in MT elimination. In C. elegans, previous studies have shown that the Efa6 protein and the MTED domain function in limiting MT growth at the cell cortex in dividing cells (O'Rourke et al., 2010) and that Efa6 functions in axon regeneration through interactions with MT-associated proteins Tac-1 and Zyg-8 (doublecortin-like kinase) (Chen et al., 2011; 2015). Thus, this study adds to the literature by showing Efa6 and its MTED also function in axon outgrowth, branch formation and maintenance in a similar manner and provide evidence that Efa6 cooperates with Shot protein to accomplish these tasks. Shot appears to act, shown through previous studies by this lab, as a MT bundle organizer and Efa6 is proposed to work as a quality control mechanism to keep MTs from going off track. The major concern of this reviewer is how much this study really adds to our understanding of Efa6 function in the nervous system. The protein was already known to limit MT polymerization at the plasma membrane and the MTED was previously shown to be critical for this function, both in non-neuronal cells and neurons. Yes, this work adds to the literature by showing Efa6 also acts in axon outgrowth, branching and maintenance but the authors are not able to determine the mechanism of action. Thus, this seems to be an incremental advance.

Reviewer #2:

Qu et al. investigate Drosophila Efa6 in neurons and show that reduction in Efa6 results in an increase in axon length and more branches, while overexpression of Efa6 has the opposite phenotype. Further, Efa6 reduction results in more axonal swellings and some of these contain disorganised microtubules. Overexpression of Efa6 or of N-terminal fragments containing the so-called microtubule elimination domain (MTED) in fibroblasts reduces MTs at the cell cortex. These data are nice and convincing, but in line with previous findings in C. elegans (O'Rourke et al., 2010 and Chen et al., 2015). Thus, the study largely corroborates previous findings. Unfortunately, a conceptual advance how Efa6 functions is lacking, mainly because the attempt to reconstitute the proposed process of cortex-induced catastrophe with purified proteins failed. This is probably not surprising as interacting partners of the 18 amino acid MTED have already been identified by others (Chen et al., 2015), which could mediate microtubule-regulating functions. While it might not be absolutely necessary to reconstitute the effect in vitro, the cell biology experiments provided are also lacking mechanistic insight as most only show a snapshot of defects after several days of inhibition/overexpression. The high-resolution imaging possible in the fibroblasts experiments has not been employed to study the interactions of Efa6 with microtubules at the cell cortex and thus to provide direct evidence that and new insight how Efa6 eliminates off-track microtubules.

Essential revisions:

1) It is unclear why the authors used lower amounts of Efa6 in their in vitro assays than MCAK even though they show that Efa6 binds weaker to microtubules than MCAK. Also, why would the authors assume that Efa6 could depolymerise GMPCPP-stabilised microtubules? Surely one would try to see an effect on dynamic microtubules first. If the proposal is that Efa6 triggers catastrophe at the cell cortex, then slowing down assembly is all what it takes to have the desired effect. Further, it seems dangerous to lyophilise and then reconstitute purified Efa6 in water. While this might be appropriate for some proteins, I wouldn't want to conclude that a protein has no effect on microtubule dynamics unless I used at least once a fresh prep of protein. Thus, I am not convinced that we can take the manuscript as negative evidence for a direct function of Efa6 on microtubules.

2) The authors propose that shot causes more off track MTs and Efa6 removes them. This is testable by expressing Efa6 in shot mutants, which should correct the defects. Shot mutants should increase the incidents of off track MTs whose interactions with Efa6 could then be studied more easily, ideally by recruiting Efa6 locally and determining the cortex dwell times of off track MTs in the Efa6 positive regions relative to normal or depleted cell cortex.

3) The number of EBs and filopodia per neuron or growth cone will depend at least partially on its size. Thus as neurons are small and don't have a proper growth cone when Efa6 is overexpressed (Figure 6G,H), it is expected that the numbers of other items are also reduced and vice versa in Efa6 mutants. The data in Figure 6 and Figure 7 need to be shown relative to neuron size / axon length / growth cone (surface) area. The distributions should be shown also for the control and actual values presented. For example, lifetime should be given in seconds and speed in nm/s, counts as a frequency per µm of axon or µm2 of growth cone. The authors will need to reassess whether statistically significant effects are present once the data have been normalised correctly.

4) Distributions or error bars are missing for a number of panels. Count data with two categories do not need to be shown as stacked bars, but should rather contain error bars or the exact values for technical repeats / independent experiments. Some data are just mentioned in the text. In particular, dwell times of microtubule tips at the cell cortex are key given the title of the manuscript, but no quantitative data are shown in the figures.

Reviewer #3:

This work is a comprehensive study on the function of efa6 in regulating axonal growth and axonal maintenance. It uses a combination of systems to conclude that Drosophila (and C. elegans, together with published work) efa6 may be a cortical MT collapse factor eliminating MTs that have left the axon bundle (but that its function is not conserved in vertebrates).

The phenotypes regarding axon length, and MT organization and/or levels are quite striking, both in flies and in fibroblasts. However, it is a pity that the mechanism of action is not clarified, especially since MTED had already been described to have such a function in C. elegans. I am not sure the data has eliminated the possibility of efa6 having an effect on the biophysics of the membrane/cortex, and this effect indirectly impacting on MTs. Could the authors discuss this?

Can the authors explain why they analyzed efa6 in the first place? It is not described in the Introduction what was the argument for this study.

An extremely dense paper, where it feels on occasions that the authors want to present everything they have tested, which makes some parts of the manuscript difficult to read. I would suggest the shortening/reduction of some sections. For example, the domain characterization could start with MTED, since this domain has already been shown to have a MT destabilizing function in C. elegans, and the C. elegans efa6 has no PDZ domain, for example.

The domain analysis was done in the presence of endogenous protein, so it is harder to conclude what the primary function of the domain is, as the phenotypes can result from complex dominant effects, or they may rely on the endogenous full length. For the key domains, would it be possible to test the effect in the absence of endogenous prot? Maybe transfecting primary cultured neurons from the mutant flies? For example, what happens when the only efa6 protein expressed in cells is a full length one with a mutated MTED?

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled "Efa6 protects axons and regulates their growth and branching by inhibiting microtubule polymerisation at the cortex" for consideration at eLife. Your article and your letter of appeal and response to referee comments have been considered by a Senior Editor, a reviewing editor, and three referees of your original submission, and we regret to inform you that we are upholding our original decision.

Please note that the referees believe your work is improved, but is not sufficiently rigorous in many instances due to missing controls and analysis (noted by the referees in the comments below) to provide mechanistic Efa6 functions in microtubule regulation. There have also been a number of issues raised about the writing and more importantly referencing key papers in the field.

Reviewer #1:

I think that the paper has improved significantly mainly by shortening the writing, however, major issues remain and I don't feel that my previous comments have been adequately addressed in the revised version.

Note: As I feel that reviewers should not be expected to download and consider data from an author's private website, I did not take into consideration the source data tables nor the supplementary movies that were not uploaded together with the manuscript. However, I don't expect that their availability would have changed my conclusions significantly.

The authors now claim to have directly shown that MTED blocks MT growth in vitro and in cells, thereby providing new mechanistic insight. The data that supposedly show this are provided in a minimalistic Figure 4 and a supplementary movie which wasn't available on the journal's website.

The "successful" in vitro experiments were done with equimolar and a tenfold excess of MTED peptide to tubulin. It is highly unlikely that 30 – 300 μm MTED is physiologically relevant and the observed effect might not even be specific. An adequate control for this experiment would be to show that a scrambled peptide does not have a similar effect at this concentration. As the authors have a Efa6::GFP knock-in line, it should be possible to determine the endogenous concentration of Efa6 relative to a GFP standard and then repeat in vitro experiments at physiologically relevant peptide concentrations including an adequate control. Furthermore, the results should be quantified in order to sustain the claim in subsection “The MTED is a good predictor of MT-inhibiting function directly affecting MT polymerisation”: "resulted in strong suppression of MT polymerisation in a dose-dependent manner". The figure only shows a single snapshot of Taxol-stabilised MTs. Polymerisation itself has not been measured or visualised for either concentration of MTED peptide. In light of the data supporting a direct role of Efa6 MTED towards microtubules being so weak, I repeat that it would be appropriate to discuss previously published findings of Efa6 interactors that are known to interact with microtubules and might work together with Efa6 to affect microtubule assembly in the vicinity of the cell cortex. Given the SxIP related motifs in Efa6, EBs are additional potential interactors that have been implicated in regulating microtubule dynamics at the cell cortex before.

The requested data describing microtubule behaviour in Efa6-expressing fibroblasts were not provided beyond a statement referring to a supplementary movie. As those are key to the mechanistic understanding of Efa6 action and for supporting a key claim in the manuscript title, data need to be provided in a main figure or table and include a robust quantification of the phenomenon.

Therefore, the manuscript still falls short in providing convincing evidence for Efa6 to inhibit microtubule polymerisation at the cell cortex.

There are several incidences of overstatement / oversimplification, e.g.:

1) The data in Figure 3B show that overexpression of Efa6-Nterm-ΔMTED has a significant effect on axon loss. This is weaker than that of Efa6-Nterm or of Efa6-FL, but it is still statistically significant, suggesting that there is residual activity in that fragment. Likewise, in fibroblasts, Efa6-Nterm-ΔMTED results in complete loss of microtubules in a few cells, which did not happen in the GFP control. However, the authors state in subsection “The N-terminal 18aa motif of Efa6 is essential for microtubule-436 inhibiting activity of Efa6”: "Efa6-Nterm-ΔMTED::GFP behaved like GFP controls". The statements should be corrected and any additional activity towards microtubules outside of the MTED region should be discussed.

2) The data in Figure 3C-D show that human full length PSD1-3 have a significant effect on microtubules (p=0.001!!!), but the authors state in subsection “The MTED is a good predictor of MT-inhibiting function directly affecting MT polymerisation”: "none of the 6 human constructs.… showed MT collapse (Figure 3C-E)". Actually, the effect of the full-length PSD constructs cannot be matched by the N-terminal portion of the molecules or the MTED-like region in the human proteins. This discrepancy should be described and discussed rather than hidden in the paper.

Comments on writing and data presentation:

1) The paper suffers from an inadequately high rate of self-citations, while lacking balanced representation of other work in the field. One example is the citing of two review articles and a preprint involving the senior author for the statement in the Introduction: "Here we make use of Drosophila neurons as a well-established, powerful model for studying roles of MT regulators". This statement should instead be followed by references to landmark papers in the field in which key discoveries were first described.

2) The figures don't align with the text. Some panels are never cited and those that are cited are in random order, for example Figure S3 (now Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and Figure S5 (now Figure 3—figure supplement 2)are cited well before Figure S1 (now Figure 3—figure supplement 5) and Figure S2 (now Figure 3—figure supplement 4) are mentioned. Figure 2D is cited before Figure 1A-C or 2A-C were mentioned etc.

3) The figure legends lack structure and information on the number of independent experiments from which the data were obtained – the methods section doesn't provide this information either for the majority of the experiments. Any raw data to be considered should be uploaded with the manuscript as supplementary information. The authors need to state for each panel what the sample number refers to: individual measurements, cells/embryos analysed or independent experimental repeats.

4) There is unnecessary reference to methods and papers where methods have been used before in the Results section … and specific bar colours within the main text (e.g. Results section and Discussion section), reducing readability.

5) The methods section does not contain sufficient information without needing to refer to a whole lot of the lab's previous papers. For example, in subsection “Drosophila primary cell culture”: "per 100 μl dispersion medium (Prokop et al., 2012)" even the composition of media is not included.

6) The authors should explain the differences between the various Efa6 mutant strains used and a rationale why certain experiments were done with only one particular strain. For example, why is EB1 comet lifetime in filopodia shown for GX6[w+], but in growth cones for GX6[w-]? Why are filopodia per growth cone with Eb1 comets shown for GX6[w-] and KO#1, but filopodia per growth cone with MTs for GX6[w-] and GX6[w+], but not for the KO line? One can't help to suspect that data that didn't fit the scheme were excluded. If this isn't the case, the authors should provide an explanation for the inconsistencies.

Reviewer #2:

In my previous review my main concern was how much this study really adds to our understanding of Efa6 function in the nervous system. The protein was already known to limit MT polymerization at the plasma membrane and the microtubule elimination domain (MTED) was previously shown to be critical for this function, both in non-neuronal cells and neurons. The authors have now added new data (Figures 4, Figure 6G and Figure 8N). Importantly, Figure 4 shows that the MTED peptide is capable of limiting MT polymerization in vitro when only tubulin and MTED peptide is present. Furthermore, they show that the MTED peptide is able to immunoprecipitate purified tubulin. These experiments suggest that the MTED can function directly with tubulin. These data do provide some mechanism that was lacking in the previous version of the manuscript. However, it is somewhat crude to compare MTED inhibition of polymerization to no addition of MTED (in the growth assay in Figure 4A) or by comparing MTED-coupled beads to empty beads (in the IP in Figure 4B). These are very weak negative controls, given that tubulin readily interacts non-specifically with other proteins in many assays and there are not any positive controls in the assays they perform in Figure 4. In Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B they use MCAK in their in vitro assays as a positive control. Since the Efa6-δ-Cterminal peptide does not seem to work in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A/B (the authors suggest this may be due to large disordered regions in that part of the protein), some other (scrambled?) peptide could be used as a negative control and/or MCAK (or peptide thereof) as a positive control. Such experiments would provide a more compelling mechanism with relatively little additional work. Additionally, the authors have also modified the previous manuscript to make it more coherent and compact and addressed my previous minor concerns.

Reviewer #3:

This work is a comprehensive study on the function and molecular mechanism of efa6 in regulating MT organization during axonal growth and axonal maintenance. It uses a combination of systems to conclude that Drosophila efa6 is a cortical MT collapse factor blocking growth of MTs that have left the axon bundle (but that its function is not conserved in vertebrates). The authors have answered most of the points I raised in a previous review, and the manuscript has improved greatly, especially regarding the possible mechanism of efa6 action.

The only comment is that the order of Figures is slightly mixed, as in it would be better to start the results with Figure 1A, instead of Figure 1F, and the first figure supplement I encountered was Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, instead of Figure S1 (now Figure 3—figure supplement 5. In addition, there are various typos and unclear sentences, e.g., subsection “The MTED is a good predictor of MT-inhibiting function directly affecting MT polymerisation”.

claims.claim: The dwell time of Eb1 comets at filopodial tips is approximately 3-fold increased in Efa6 mutant neurons compared to wild-type.
claims.source: Comet velocity was unaffected (~0.14 μm/s), but the lifetime of Eb1::GFP comets (5.04 s ± 0.60 SEM in wild-type) was ~1.4 times longer in mutant GCs, with the dwell time of Eb1 comets at the tip of filopodia being ~3 fold increased (from 2.10 s ± 0.24 SEM in wild-type to 6.26 s± 0.40 SEM in Efa6 mutant neurons; Figure 5M)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of Eb1 comet dwell times at filopodial tips comparing wild-type and Efa6 mutant neurons.

claims.claim: More microtubules are found in growth cone filopodia in Efa6 mutant neurons compared to wild-type.
claims.source: In agreement with the increased lifetime, more MTs were found in growth cone filopodia in Efa6 mutant neurons, as quantified by counting filopodia that contained EB1 comets or MTs (Figure 5J,K and arrow heads in D,E; note that the total number of filopodia per GC was in the range of 10–11 for both wild-type and Efa6; not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia containing MTs or EB1 comets in wild-type versus Efa6 mutant neurons.

claims.claim: Transgenic expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduces the number of growth cone filopodia containing Eb1 comets or MTs.
claims.source: Transgenically expressed Efa6-FL::GFP caused the opposite effect, that is a reduction in the number of GC filopodia containing Eb1 comets or MTs (Figure 5G–L; green columns in I-L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing reduced filopodial MTs in neurons over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP.

claims.claim: Loss or gain of Efa6 function has no obvious effect on Eb1 comet numbers, lifetimes, velocities, and directionalities in axon shafts.
claims.source: Next, we investigated MT dynamics in axon shafts. In contrast to GCs, MTs in the axon shaft are organised into bundles, hence kept away from the membrane. Accordingly, neither loss- nor gain-of-function had an obvious effect on Eb1 comet numbers, lifetimes, velocities and directionalities (Figure 6A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of multiple MT dynamic parameters in axon shafts showing no significant changes upon Efa6 manipulation.

claims.claim: Loss of Efa6 causes a strong increase in axon shaft filopodia containing MTs.
claims.source: However, like in GCs, there was a strong increase in filopodia along the shaft that contained MTs when Efa6 was absent, and a strong decrease when over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of shaft filopodia containing MTs in Efa6 loss-of-function conditions.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Efa6-FL::GFP causes a strong decrease in axon shaft filopodia containing MTs.
claims.source: However, like in GCs, there was a strong increase in filopodia along the shaft that contained MTs when Efa6 was absent, and a strong decrease when over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of shaft filopodia containing MTs in Efa6 over-expression conditions.

claims.claim: Efa6 primarily inhibits explorative MTs that leave the axon bundle in either growth cones or axon shafts and polymerize towards the cell membrane or into filopodia.
claims.source: Taken together, our data are consistent with a model in which Efa6 primarily inhibits explorative MTs that leave the axon bundle in either GCs or axon shafts and polymerise towards the cell membrane or into filopodia.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive data showing Efa6 effects on MTs specifically in growth cones and filopodia but not in axon shaft bundles.

claims.claim: Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons show almost double the number of collateral branches compared to wild-type neurons at 5 days in vitro.
claims.source: We found that Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons showed almost double the number of collateral branches as observed in wild-type neurons, whereas expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduced branching by 21% (Figure 7A–C,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in mature cultured neurons comparing Efa6 mutant to wild-type.

claims.claim: Expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduces axonal branching by 21% in cultured neurons at 5 days in vitro.
claims.source: We found that Efa6KO#1 homozygous mutant neurons showed almost double the number of collateral branches as observed in wild-type neurons, whereas expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduced branching by 21% (Figure 7A–C,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in mature cultured neurons over-expressing Efa6-FL::GFP.

claims.claim: Expression of Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX causes a similar degree of branch reduction as Efa6-FL::GFP.
claims.source: This reduction is mediated by the Efa6 N-terminus, since expression of Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX caused a similar degree in branch reduction (Figure 7D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of branching phenotypes between Efa6-FL::GFP and Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX expressing neurons.

claims.claim: Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons causes a 29% increase in branch numbers in young brains and 38% increase in old brains.
claims.source: We found that Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons caused a significant increase in branch numbers by 29% in young and by 38% in old brains, whereas over-expression of Efa6::GFP strongly decreased branch numbers by 33% in young and 28% in old brains, respectively (Figure 7L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in dorsal cluster neurons in vivo at different ages with Efa6 knock-down.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Efa6::GFP in dorsal cluster neurons decreases branch numbers by 33% in young brains and 28% in old brains.
claims.source: We found that Efa6 knock-down in dorsal cluster neurons caused a significant increase in branch numbers by 29% in young and by 38% in old brains, whereas over-expression of Efa6::GFP strongly decreased branch numbers by 33% in young and 28% in old brains, respectively (Figure 7L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of branch numbers in dorsal cluster neurons in vivo at different ages with Efa6 over-expression.

claims.claim: Only 57% of young brains expressing Efa6-FL::GFP in dorsal cluster neurons had axons in the medulla region, compared to 88% in controls.
claims.source: In these experiments, Efa6-FL::GFP expression had an intriguing further effect: Only 57% of young brains had any axons in the medulla region, compared to 88% in controls, whereas the axons were eventually present in the older Efa6-FL::GFP expressing fly brains (Figure 7H,K,M, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon presence in medulla regions of young brains with Efa6-FL::GFP expression.

claims.claim: Efa6 acts as a negative regulator of axonal branching mediated through its N-terminus.
claims.source: Taken together, our data indicate a physiologically relevant role for Efa6 as negative regulator of axonal branching, mediated through its N-terminus, most likely via its function as cortical collapse factor.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive data from cultured neurons and in vivo experiments showing branching phenotypes upon Efa6 manipulation.

claims.claim: Efa6-depleted neurons display axons with swellings where MTs lose their bundled conformation and are arranged into intertwined, criss-crossing curls.
claims.source: Apart from changes in growth and branching, we noticed that a significant amount of Efa6-depleted neurons displayed axons with swellings where MTs lost their bundled conformation and were arranged into intertwined, criss-crossing curls instead (arrowheads in Figure 8D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations of MT organization in axons of Efa6-depleted neurons.

claims.claim: MT disorganization in Efa6 mutant neurons shows a mild 1.3-fold increase at 6 hours in vitro, worsening to 2.3-fold at 5 days and approximately 4-fold at 10 days.
claims.source: MDI measurements in Efa6 mutant neurons revealed a mild 1.3 fold increase in MT disorganisation in young neurons which gradually worsened to 2.3 fold at 5 DIV and ~4 fold at 10 DIV (Figure 8A–F,I; all normalised to controls).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements at multiple time points showing progressive worsening of MT disorganization.

claims.claim: Pre-culture strategy to remove maternal Efa6 still results in low MT disorganization in young neurons with gradual increase over subsequent days.
claims.source: To assess the latter possibility, we used a pre-culture strategy to remove potential maternal Efa6 (see Materials and methods for details; Prokop et al., 2012; Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2010). When plating neurons after 5 days of pre-culture, we still found a low amount of MT disorganisation in young neurons and a subsequent gradual increase to severe phenotypes over the following days (Figure 8J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using pre-culture to eliminate maternal contribution, showing persistent MT disorganization phenotype.

claims.claim: Efa6 is required during later maintenance stages to prevent MT disorganization, as shown by conditional knock-down experiments.
claims.source: After this period, cells were grown for another four days under knock-down conditions (27°C), and then fixed on day seven. At this point, MT disorganisation in the elav/Efa6IR/Gal80ts neurons was significantly increased over control neurons (Figure 8K), indicating that Efa6 is not only required during development but also during later maintenance to prevent MT disorganisation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by temporal control experiments showing that Efa6 knock-down in mature neurons causes MT disorganization.

claims.claim: Expression of Efa6-FL::GFP or Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX shows a tendency to reduce MT disorganization below baseline levels in control cells.
claims.source: In contrast to increased MT disorganisation upon functional loss of Efa6, expression of Efa6-FL::GFP or Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX showed a tendency to reduce MT disorganisation even below the baseline levels measured in control cells (cultured in parallel without the expression construct; Figure 8I), suggesting that also this role of Efa6 is likely due to the cortical collapse function of Efa6 (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements in neurons over-expressing Efa6 constructs.

claims.claim: Efa6 knock-down in lamina neurons causes a doubling in the occurrence of axonal swellings with disorganized MTs in aged flies.
claims.source: When analysing aged flies at 26–27 days, we found that Efa6 knock-down caused a doubling in the occurrence of axonal swellings with disorganised axonal MTs: the average of total swellings per column section was increased from 0.3 in controls to 0.65 swellings upon Efa6 knock-down; about a third of these contained disorganised MTs (GMR-tub-Efa6IR: 0.23 per column section; GMR-tub: 0.13; Figure 9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axonal swellings and MT disorganization in aged fly brains with Efa6 knock-down.

claims.claim: Efa6 provides a quality control mechanism that prevents MT disorganization by inhibiting only MTs that have escaped axonal bundles.
claims.source: We propose therefore that Efa6 provides a quality control mechanism that prevents MT disorganisation by inhibiting only MTs that have escaped axonal bundles. This model would also be consistent with the slow onset and gradual increase of MT disorganisation we observed upon Efa6 deficiency (Figure 8I,J).
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model supported by the gradual onset of MT disorganization phenotypes and the specific effects on off-track MTs.

claims.claim: Both shot3 and Efa6GX6[w-] single-mutant conditions show a strong enhancement of filopodial MTs, which is substantially further increased in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double-mutant neurons.
claims.source: To study potential mutual enhancement of Efa6 and shot mutant phenotypes, we first determined numbers of MTs in axonal shaft filopodia: both single-mutant conditions showed a strong enhancement of filopodial MTs (blue vs. orange bars in Figure 6F,G); this phenotype was substantially further increased in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double-mutant neurons (orange/blue bars in Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of filopodial MTs in single and double mutant conditions showing additive effects.

claims.claim: Transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP significantly improves the shot3 mutant phenotype of filopodial MTs.
claims.source: Vice versa, when transfecting Efa6-FL-GFP to boost the hypothesised 'cleaning-up' function, the shot3 mutant phenotype was significantly improved (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis showing reduced filopodial MTs in shot3 mutant neurons upon Efa6-FL-GFP expression.

claims.claim: At 6 hours in vitro, shot3 mutant neurons display a 2.4-fold increase in MDI, Efa6GX6[w-] mutant neurons a 1.55-fold increase, and shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double mutant neurons a 6.16-fold increase.
claims.source: At 6 HIV, shot3 mutant neurons displayed a 2.4-fold, and Efa6GX6[w-] mutant neurons a 1.55-fold increase in MDI (normalised to wild-type); this value was dramatically increased to 6.16 fold in shot3 Efa6GX6[w-] double mutant neurons (Figure 8M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements in single and double mutant conditions showing synergistic effects.

claims.claim: Transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP into shot3 mutant neurons alleviates the MDI phenotype.
claims.source: This conclusion was further confirmed by our finding that transfection of Efa6-FL-GFP into shot3 mutant neurons could alleviate the MDI phenotype (Figure 8N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements showing rescue of shot3 phenotype by Efa6-FL-GFP expression.

claims.claim: MT disorganization phenotypes of Efa6-RNAi and shot3/+ heterozygous mutant neurons are enhanced when both genetic manipulations are combined.
claims.source: Since complete loss of Shot is an embryonically lethal condition, we first tested in culture whether the lack of just one copy of shot has an enhancing effect on Efa6 deficiency. We found that MT disorganisation phenotypes of Efa6-RNAi (blue bar in Figure 8L) and of shot3/+ heterozygous mutant neurons (orange bar) at 6 HIV were clearly enhanced when both genetic manipulations were combined (orange/blue bar).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative MDI measurements showing enhanced phenotypes in combined Efa6 and shot heterozygous conditions.

claims.claim: Cell-autonomous knock-down of Efa6 in a shot3/+ heterozygous mutant background further enhances MT disorganization in the optic lobe compared to Efa6 knock-down alone.
claims.source: When testing the same genetic constellations in our optic lobe model, we found that the originally observed increase in MT disorganisation caused by cell-autonomous knock-down of Efa6 (black arrows and blue bar in Figure 9B,E) was also further enhanced when the same experiment was carried out in a shot3/+ heterozygous mutant background (black arrows and orange/blue bar in Figure 9C,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo quantitative analysis of MT disorganization in optic lobe showing genetic interaction between Efa6 and shot.

claims.claim: Shot and Efa6 regulate axonal MTs through independent and complementary pathways.
claims.source: These findings support our conclusion that there is a correlation between off-track MTs and MT disorganisation. Furthermore, they are consistent with a scenario where both Shot and Efa6 regulate axonal MTs but through independent and complementary pathways: Efa6 inhibits MTs at the cortex (with peripheral MTs persisting for longer if Efa6 is absent), whereas Shot actively maintains MTs in bundles (with more MTs going off-track if Shot is absent) - and both these functions complement each other during MT bundle maintenance and enhance each other's mutant phenotypes in double-mutant conditions (see further details in the Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model supported by genetic interaction data showing additive and synergistic effects of shot and Efa6 mutations.

claims.claim: Cortical collapse factors are important microtubule regulators relevant for axon morphology.
claims.source: Cortical collapse factors are important microtubule regulators relevant for axon morphology
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: C. elegans Efa6 negatively impacts on developmental and regenerative axon growth.
claims.source: the ARF activator Efa6 (exchange factor for ARF6) in C. elegans negatively impacts on developmental and regenerative axon growth (Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011; O'Rourke et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Mammalian KIF21A affects axon growth and links to congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles.
claims.source: the mammalian type four kinesin KIF21A also affects axon growth and links to the neurodevelopmental eye movement disorder 'congenital fibrosis of extraocular muscles' (OMIM reference #135700; Heidary et al., 2008; Tiab et al., 2004; van der Vaart et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and clinical database references.

claims.claim: Growth cones are amoeboid tip structures through which axons extend during development or regeneration.
claims.source: GCs are the amoeboid tip structures through which axons extend to wire the nervous system during development or regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about growth cone structure and function.

claims.claim: Explorative MTs in growth cones can trigger extension of the entire MT bundle, thus elongating the axon.
claims.source: The axonal MT bundles terminate in the centre of GCs; from here, single MTs splay into the actin-rich periphery of GCs. These explorative MTs can trigger extension of the entire MT bundle into their direction, thus elongating the axon (Dent et al., 2011; Lowery and Vactor, 2009; Prokop et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing growth cone mechanisms.

claims.claim: Collateral branching of axons depends on explorative MTs that leave parallel axonal bundles and polymerize towards the periphery.
claims.source: for example, collateral branching of axons along their shafts has been described to depend on explorative MTs that leave the parallel axonal bundles and polymerise towards the periphery (Kalil and Dent, 2014; Lewis et al., 2013; Tymanskyj et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on axon branching mechanisms.

claims.claim: The model of 'local axon homeostasis' states that the force-enriched environment in axons biases MTs to buckle or project out of the bundle to seed pathological areas of MT disorganization.
claims.source: the model of 'local axon homeostasis' states that the force-enriched environment in axons biases MTs to buckle or project out of the bundle to seed pathological areas of MT disorganisation (Hahn et al., 2019; Prokop, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim describes a published theoretical model supported by citations.

claims.claim: Spectraplakins serve as spacers that keep polymerizing MTs away from the cortex by linking MT tips to the axonal surface and guiding them into parallel bundles.
claims.source: For example, spectraplakins serve as spacers that keep polymerising MTs away from the cortex by linking the tips of extending MTs to the axonal surface and guiding them into parallel bundles (Alves-Silva et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work on spectraplakin function.

claims.claim: Deficiency of spectraplakins causes severe MT disorganization and is linked to human HSAN6.
claims.source: Their deficiency in any organism causes severe MT disorganisation, potentially explaining human dystonin-linked HSAN6 ('type six hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy''; OMIM ID: 614653; Voelzmann et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work and clinical database reference.

claims.claim: Drosophila neurons are a well-established, powerful model for studying roles of MT regulators.
claims.source: Here, we make use of Drosophila neurons as a well-established, powerful model for studying roles of MT regulators (He and Roblodowski, 2016; Nye et al., 2014; Prokop et al., 2013; Sánchez-Soriano et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature establishing Drosophila as a model system.

claims.claim: Drosophila Efa6 can inhibit MTs directly without interacting molecules via an N-terminal 18 amino acid motif (MTED) that binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule growth in vitro and cells.
claims.source: First, we show that Drosophila Efa6 can inhibit MTs directly without interacting molecules via an N-terminal 18 amino acid motif (MT elimination domain/MTED) that binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule growth in vitro and cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assays, MT growth assays, and cellular experiments presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: N-terminal MTED-containing fragments in the cytoplasm abolish entire microtubule networks of mouse fibroblasts and whole axons of fly neurons.
claims.source: If N-terminal MTED-containing fragments are in the cytoplasm they abolish entire microtubule networks of mouse fibroblasts and whole axons of fly neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of cytoplasmic MTED-containing constructs on MT networks.

claims.claim: Full-length Efa6 is membrane-attached and primarily blocks MTs in the periphery of fibroblasts and explorative MTs that have left axonal bundles in neurons.
claims.source: Full-length Efa6 is membrane-attached, hence primarily blocks MTs in the periphery of fibroblasts, and explorative MTs that have left axonal bundles in neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by localization studies and functional analyses showing membrane association and selective MT inhibition.

claims.claim: Loss of Efa6 causes an increase of explorative MTs in growth cones that enhance axon growth and in axon shafts that cause excessive branching and atrophy through perturbations of MT bundles.
claims.source: Accordingly, loss of Efa6 causes an increase of explorative MTs: in growth cones they enhance axon growth, in axon shafts they cause excessive branching, as well as atrophy through perturbations of MT bundles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive experimental data on axon growth, branching, and MT organization in Efa6 loss-of-function conditions.

claims.claim: Efa6 over-expression causes phenotypes opposite to loss of function.
claims.source: Efa6 over-expression causes the opposite phenotypes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced axon growth, reduced branching, and reduced MT disorganization upon Efa6 over-expression.

claims.claim: The MTED delivers a promising tool that can be used to inhibit MTs in a compartmentalized fashion when fused to specifically localizing protein domains.
claims.source: Furthermore, the MTED delivers a promising tool that can be used to inhibit MTs in a compartmentalised fashion when fusing it to specifically localising protein domains.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with CAAX-tagged constructs showing that MTED function can be spatially controlled through localization domains.

claims.claim: Axons are 0.1–15 µm in diameter but can be up to a meter long in humans.
claims.source: They are only 0.1–15 µm in diameter (Hoffman, 1995), but can be up to a meter long in humans (Debanne et al., 2011; Prokop, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on axon dimensions.

claims.claim: Humans gradually lose about 40% of axons towards old age.
claims.source: It is not surprising that we gradually lose about 40% of our axons towards old age (Calkins, 2013; Marner et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on age-related axon loss.

claims.claim: Axon decay is a prominent neurodegenerative phenomenon.
claims.source: and that axon decay is a prominent neurodegenerative phenomenon (Adalbert and Coleman, 2013; Fang and Bonini, 2012; Medana and Esiri, 2003; Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: Parallel bundles of microtubules running along the axon shaft provide structural support, highways for cargo transport, and a source of MTs for morphogenetic changes.
claims.source: Essential for axon biology are the parallel bundles of microtubules (MTs) running all along the axon shaft; these bundles provide (1) structural support, (2) highways for life-sustaining cargo transport, and (3) a source of MTs that can leave these bundles to drive morphogenetic changes.
claims.evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about MT bundle functions in axons.

claims.claim: MTs essentially drive processes of axon growth, branching and maintenance through their organization in parallel bundles.
claims.source: Through being organised in this way, MTs essentially drive processes of axon growth, branching and maintenance (Conde and Cáceres, 2009; Dent et al., 2011; Prokop, 2013; Voelzmann et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature on MT functions in axons.

results.result: Efa6 is widely expressed throughout the Drosophila nervous system at both larval and adult stages, and localizes throughout cell bodies and axons in cultured primary neurons at both young (6 hours in vitro) and mature (5 days in vitro) stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are supported by direct experimental evidence using a genomically engineered GFP-tagged Efa6 line. The expression pattern is documented in CNS tissue at multiple developmental stages (Figure 1A-D) and in cultured neurons at different time points (Figure 1E,F,H,I), providing consistent evidence for widespread expression and subcellular localization.

results.result: Efa6 negatively regulates axon length in Drosophila primary neurons: loss of Efa6 increases axon length by at least 20% at 6 hours in vitro, while over-expression of Efa6-FL::GFP reduces axon length by approximately 20% (transgenic) to 50% (transfected) and increases the percentage of neurons without axons from ~26% to ~43%.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 are well-supported by quantitative measurements of axon length in multiple Efa6 loss-of-function and gain-of-function conditions (Figure 2). The bidirectional effects (loss-of-function increases, gain-of-function decreases) provide strong evidence for Efa6's role as a negative regulator of axon growth. Statistical significance is reported for all conditions.

results.result: Efa6-FL::GFP expression in fibroblasts causes dose-dependent depletion of microtubule networks, with the protein localizing to the cell periphery at low/moderate expression levels (where MTs are lost from cell fringes) and becoming cytoplasmic/nuclear at high expression levels (where prominent MT networks are completely lost). Live imaging shows that growing MTs extend to cell fringes in controls but stop at the border of Efa6-FL::GFP-enriched zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by comprehensive microscopy data in fibroblasts showing graded MT depletion correlated with Efa6 expression levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and live imaging demonstrating MT exclusion from Efa6-enriched zones (Figure 4, Animations 1-2). The dose-dependent effects and dynamic behavior provide strong evidence for Efa6's MT-inhibiting function at the cell cortex.

results.result: The 18 amino acid MTED motif is the key mediator of Drosophila Efa6's MT-depleting functions: only constructs containing the MTED cause strong axon loss in neurons and MT network depletion in fibroblasts, while mutation of both SxIP motifs does not prevent these effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C12, and C14 are strongly supported by systematic structure-function analyses comparing multiple Efa6 constructs with and without the MTED or with mutated SxIP motifs (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3). The data clearly demonstrate that the MTED is necessary and sufficient for MT-depleting activity, while SxIP motifs are dispensable, establishing the MTED as the key functional domain.

results.result: The presence of a well-conserved canonical MTED predicts MT-inhibiting capabilities of Efa6 family members: all six fly/worm Efa6 constructs tested had strong MT-inhibiting properties in fibroblasts, while six human PSD constructs showed only slight MT network defects and never caused complete MT network depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are supported by comparative functional analyses of Efa6 orthologs from multiple species (Figure 3C-E). The correlation between MTED presence and strong MT-inhibiting activity across species provides strong evidence for the MTED as a predictor of function. However, the evolutionary analysis could be strengthened with more detailed sequence comparisons and functional validation of the divergent human sequences.

results.result: The MTED directly interacts with tubulin and interferes with MT polymerization: purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP associates with MTs in vitro but does not depolymerize them; synthetic MTED peptide reduces MT polymer production by ~10-fold in vitro (while scrambled peptide has no effect); and MTED-coated beads pull down 3-5 times more tubulin than uncoated or scrambled peptide-coated beads.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C25 are supported by multiple complementary in vitro assays (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The MT binding assays, growth inhibition assays, and pull-down experiments provide converging evidence for direct MTED-tubulin interaction and MT polymerization inhibition. The use of scrambled peptide controls strengthens the specificity argument. However, the failure of purified Efa6-Nterm::GFP to depolymerize MTs suggests potential issues with recombinant protein preparation that are acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: The C-terminal domain of Efa6 restricts MT-inhibiting activity to the cortex through membrane association: Efa6-ΔCterm::GFP and Efa6-Nterm::GFP fail to associate with the cortex and induce stronger MT phenotypes than Efa6-FL::GFP, while addition of a CAAX membrane-targeting domain to Efa6-Nterm::GFP restores Efa6-FL::GFP-like behaviors including cortical localization and moderate MT phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are strongly supported by systematic structure-function analyses comparing constructs with and without the C-terminus and with artificial membrane-targeting domains (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplements 6-7, Figure 4C-E, Animation 4). The CAAX rescue experiment is particularly compelling, demonstrating that membrane tethering is sufficient to restrict MTED function to the cortex. This establishes Efa6 as a cortical collapse factor with spatially restricted activity.

results.result: Efa6 negatively regulates MT polymerization at the growth cone membrane and in filopodia: loss of Efa6 increases total Eb1 comet numbers in growth cones, prolongs comet lifetime (~1.4-fold) and dwell time at filopodial tips (~3-fold) without affecting velocity (~0.14 μm/s), and increases the number of filopodia containing MTs, while Efa6-FL::GFP over-expression causes opposite effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 are supported by comprehensive quantitative live imaging analyses of MT dynamics in growth cones using Eb1::GFP (Figure 5, Animations 5-8). The bidirectional effects of loss- and gain-of-function manipulations, combined with multiple independent measurements (comet numbers, lifetimes, dwell times, filopodial MT content), provide strong converging evidence. The lack of effect on velocity suggests Efa6 affects MT stability/persistence rather than polymerization rate.

results.result: Efa6 primarily inhibits explorative MTs that leave axon bundles: loss or gain of Efa6 function has no obvious effect on Eb1 comet dynamics in axon shafts (where MTs are organized in bundles), but strongly affects the number of shaft filopodia containing MTs, consistent with Efa6 inhibiting explorative MTs that polymerize towards the membrane or into filopodia.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by quantitative analyses showing differential effects of Efa6 manipulation on bundled versus peripheral MTs (Figure 6A-G). The lack of effect on shaft MT dynamics combined with strong effects on filopodial MTs provides compelling evidence for the proposed model. This spatial specificity is consistent with Efa6's cortical localization and supports its role as a cortical collapse factor.

results.result: Efa6 acts as a negative regulator of axonal branching mediated through its N-terminus: Efa6KO#1 mutant neurons show almost double the branch numbers compared to wild-type at 5 days in vitro, while Efa6-FL::GFP expression reduces branching by 21% in culture and by 28-33% in vivo in dorsal cluster neurons; Efa6-Nterm::GFP::CAAX causes similar branch reduction, and Efa6-FL::GFP over-expression also delays axon outgrowth in young brains.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 are supported by quantitative branching analyses in both cultured neurons and in vivo (Figure 7). The bidirectional effects in culture, confirmation in vivo at multiple ages, and demonstration that the N-terminus is sufficient (via CAAX construct) provide strong converging evidence. The delayed outgrowth phenotype in young brains is consistent with Efa6's role in restricting axon growth. Statistical significance is reported for all conditions.

results.result: Efa6 maintains axonal MT bundle integrity in cultured neurons: Efa6-depleted neurons display axonal swellings with disorganized MTs arranged in criss-crossing curls, with MT disorganization (measured by MDI) showing a mild 1.3-fold increase at 6 hours in vitro that progressively worsens to 2.3-fold at 5 days and ~4-fold at 10 days; this phenotype persists after maternal Efa6 removal and can be induced by conditional knock-down in mature neurons, while Efa6 over-expression tends to reduce MT disorganization below baseline.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by comprehensive temporal analyses using the MDI metric (Figure 8A-K). The progressive worsening of the phenotype, persistence after maternal removal, and induction by conditional knock-down in mature neurons provide strong evidence for a continued maintenance role. However, the interpretation that Efa6 prevents MT disorganization by inhibiting off-track MTs is inferential and would benefit from direct visualization of the sequence of events.

results.result: Efa6 maintains axonal MT bundle integrity in vivo and provides a quality control mechanism: Efa6 knock-down in lamina neurons causes a doubling in axonal swellings with disorganized MTs in aged flies (26-27 days), consistent with a model where Efa6 prevents MT disorganization by inhibiting MTs that have escaped axonal bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by quantitative in vivo analyses in the optic lobe (Figure 9). The demonstration of MT disorganization in vivo validates the cultured neuron findings and establishes physiological relevance. However, C55 is a proposed model rather than directly demonstrated mechanism—the quality control function is inferred from the gradual onset and spatial specificity of phenotypes rather than directly observed.

results.result: Shot and Efa6 regulate axonal MTs through independent and complementary pathways: both shot3 and Efa6 single mutants show enhanced filopodial MTs that are substantially further increased in double mutants; shot3 mutants show 2.4-fold increased MDI and Efa6 mutants 1.55-fold, while double mutants show 6.16-fold increase; Efa6-FL-GFP over-expression significantly improves shot3 phenotypes in both filopodial MTs and MDI; and genetic interactions are confirmed in vivo in the optic lobe.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are strongly supported by comprehensive genetic interaction analyses in culture and in vivo (Figure 6F-G, Figure 8L-N, Figure 9). The additive/synergistic effects in double mutants and rescue of shot phenotypes by Efa6 over-expression provide compelling evidence for independent, complementary pathways. The proposed model (C62) that Efa6 inhibits MTs at the cortex while Shot maintains MTs in bundles is well-supported by the data, though the mechanistic details remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Efa6-Nterm::GFP tip-tracks microtubules and co-localizes with EB3::RFP at MT plus ends entering Efa6-enriched areas.
results.evaluation: Claim C13 is supported by live imaging data (Animations 2-3) showing Efa6-Nterm::GFP at MT plus ends. However, the functional significance of this tip-tracking is unclear since mutation of the SxIP motifs (which mediate EB binding) does not prevent Efa6's MT-inhibiting activity (C14), suggesting tip-tracking may not be essential for function.

results.result: Cortical collapse factors are important MT regulators relevant for axon morphology: Drosophila Efa6 can inhibit MTs directly via its N-terminal MTED that binds tubulin and inhibits MT growth; N-terminal MTED-containing fragments abolish entire MT networks when cytoplasmic, while full-length membrane-attached Efa6 primarily blocks peripheral MTs and explorative MTs; loss of Efa6 increases explorative MTs causing enhanced axon growth, excessive branching, and MT bundle perturbations, while over-expression causes opposite phenotypes; the MTED can be used as a tool for compartmentalized MT inhibition when fused to targeting domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C63, C73-C78 represent the major conceptual conclusions of the manuscript, synthesizing findings from multiple experimental approaches. These summary claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the paper. The characterization of Efa6 as a cortical collapse factor with direct MT-inhibiting activity via the MTED is strongly supported. The proposal that MTED can be used as a tool (C78) is supported by the CAAX experiments but represents future potential rather than extensive validation.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establishing the biological context for the study, including prior work on C. elegans Efa6 and mammalian KIF21A in axon growth, growth cone structure and function, axon branching mechanisms, the local axon homeostasis model, spectraplakin function, and Drosophila as a model system.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C83 represent background knowledge and prior work that provide context for the current study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to published literature and represent established knowledge in the field. The citations appear accurate and relevant, though detailed verification of each cited claim is beyond the scope of this evaluation.
